extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards for writing description, dialogue, and character in fiction: how to see, choose, and render sensory detail; how to craft honest, lifelike speech; and how to develop characters through showing and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description as sensory participation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Description is what makes the reader a sensory participant in the story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description begins with visualization of what you want the reader to experience and ends with translating what you see in your mind into words on the page. Good description is a learned skill — you must read a lot and write a lot to improve. The writer must be able to describe experiences so the reader 'prickles with recognition.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the happy medium in amount of description
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid thin description that leaves the reader bewildered and overdescription that buries the reader in irrelevant detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine 'how much' to describe by reading and practice; know what to describe and what can be left alone to keep the story moving. If descriptive material doesn't serve the story, cut or trim it in rewrite. Overindulgent description can break the spell and bore readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer locale and texture over exhaustive physical inventory
rubrics_metrics.description: Locale and texture are often more important to the reader’s sense of being in the story than catalogues of characters’ physical details or wardrobe lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid exhaustive, pimple-by-pimple or skirt-by-skirt physical descriptions that freeze out the reader’s imagination. Give enough (e.g., 'high school outcast with a bad complexion and a fashion‑victim wardrobe') so the reader can supply the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a few well-chosen details as stand-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: Good description usually consists of a few well-chosen details that will stand for everything else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the first details that come to mind when visualizing a scene are the truest and best. These salient details (sawdust on the floor, smells, a backbar mirror) can set the scene quickly and economically; you can add/delete in rewrite as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization (open all senses) before writing description
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin description by calling up an image of the place, filling the mind’s eye and opening all senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct a brief but intense memory search to capture darkness, smells, textures, noises, etc. Fact and fiction may blend in visualization; use that mixture to produce vivid, specific description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of scene-setting: 'a meal is as good as a feast'
rubrics_metrics.description: When setting a scene, less can be more; once the reader can see the location, extra descriptive material may only slow pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only what signals that the setting will matter; if it later proves irrelevant, reduce it in revision. Keep the story (what happens) the priority over descriptive flourishes that impede narrative momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative language: use fresh similes and metaphors judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of simile and other figurative language is one of the chief delights of fiction when it’s on target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ fresh images and simple vocabulary to create clarity and occasional beauty. When a simile 'works' it can make readers see an old thing in a new way; when it fails, it can be funny or embarrassing. Read widely to develop good figurative instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichéd or strained figurative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Clichéd similes, metaphors, and images make you look lazy or ignorant and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of chestnuts like 'ran like a madman' or tired comparisons. Also avoid 'Zen similes' or metaphors that make no clarifying connection (example: 'waiting for the medical examiner as patiently as a man waiting for a turkey sandwich'). Read to expose yourself to better models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue shows character (show, don't tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: "One of the cardinal rules of good fiction is never tell us a thing if you can show us, instead."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speech to reveal education, background, temperament, and values (e.g., Mistuh Butts's speech reveals lack of schooling). Dialogue can convey far more vivid information than straight narration and should be used to show rather than narrate facts about a character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue must ring true and be lifelike
rubrics_metrics.description: When dialogue is right, we know; when it’s wrong, it jags on the ear like a badly tuned musical instrument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad examples (stilted, elliptical, overwrought lines) make readers stop; good examples (natural exchanges) make readers feel they are eavesdropping. Learn dialogue by listening to others: pick up accents, rhythms, dialect, and slang. Practice builds skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest in dialogue — reflect authentic speech (including profanity when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: You must tell the truth if your dialogue is to have resonance and realism; sometimes that truth includes profanity or vulgarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sanitize characters to appease imagined censors; use words characters would really say. If a character genuinely would use euphemisms ('Oh sugar!') rather than profanity, that truth is part of characterization. The writer’s obligation is to the truth of the character and scene, not to outside moralizers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichéd or melodramatic dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Clichéd, movie-moment, or melodramatic lines (e.g., late‑forties war‑movie tropes) feel inauthentic and provoke incredulity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of using familiar dramatic turns of phrase or borrowed movie rhetoric unless deliberately intended and executed well. Editors and readers react negatively to obvious clichés; aim for original speech that serves character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character building through attention and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Building characters boils down to paying attention to how real people behave and then telling the truth about what you see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect idiosyncratic details (neighbor picks his nose) and be willing to 'dump' them into a story at the right moment. Characters are often partly you, partly observed traits, and partly imagination; combine these elements to create believable people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character growth by discovery; prioritize story over mere character study
rubrics_metrics.description: What happens to characters during a story should depend on what you discover about them as you go; the best stories end up being about the people rather than the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters may grow a little or a lot; if they grow significantly, they can begin to influence the course of the story. However, especially beyond short stories, avoid producing only a character study — the story should remain 'the boss.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Show psychological states through behavior, not labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t tell the reader a character 'was depressed'; show behaviors and let readers draw conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give readers a character’s perspective and actions (e.g., silent, dirty‑haired woman compulsively eating cake) so they can infer psychological conditions. Showing creates empathy and makes a character more frightening or sympathetic than flat, labeled portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rewrite consciously; first instincts are often valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: You should remember that it’s as easy to overdescribe as to underdescribe; rewrite exists to adjust and refine description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your first visualized details will often be the truest and best; in rewrite you can change, add, or delete. Trim descriptive passages in later drafts if they don’t serve the story’s pace or focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement comes from reading and practicing, not shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Good descriptive and dialogic skill is learned by reading much and writing much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice the art; reading exposes you to compact, powerful descriptive language (examples: Chandler, Hammett, T. S. Eliot, William Carlos Williams). Practice will never make you perfect, but it will develop your clear seeing and clear writing.
